authoredPrompt: This figure illustrates the Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) as a surface interaction model. An incoming light ray strikes a green surface at a point, where the surface normal n points upward and two ray vectors p and q define the local surface coordinate frame. Multiple outgoing arrows emanating in a hemisphere of directions represent the scattered radiance, and the governing equation shows that the reflected intensity depends on the incident radiance, surface orientation, wavelength, and surface material properties. The spread of outgoing rays captures the fact that real surfaces scatter light across many directions rather than reflecting it specularly into a single one. This figure motivates the BRDF as the general mathematical model that describes how a surface converts incoming irradiance into outgoing radiance across all viewing angles.
authoredInteractions:
- Model the BRDF live: a hemisphere of outgoing arrows above the surface point whose lengths encode reflected radiance, recomputed continuously from the current incoming direction and material
- Drag the incoming ray ℓ_in around the hemisphere: the outgoing radiance lobe re-renders in real time with the equation labels tracking
authoredContext:
A light ray from the sun strikes a surface and generates outgoing rays of intensity and color depending on the angles of the incoming and outgoing rays relative to the surface orientation.

Let an incident light ray be from direction $\mathbf{p}$ and of power,
$\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, as a function of spectral wavelength $\lambda$ ().
The power of the outgoing light, reflected in the direction,
$\mathbf{q}$, is determined by what is called the bidirectional
reflection distribution function (BRDF), $F$, of the surface. If the
surface normal is $\mathbf{n}$, then outgoing power is some function,
$F$, of the surface normal, the incoming and outgoing ray directions,
the wavelength, and the incoming light power:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{n}, \lambda, \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q} \right)
$$ {#eq-Lambert}

In general, BRDFs can be quite complicated (see ),
describing both diffuse and specular components of reflection. Even
surfaces with completely diffuse reflections can give complicated
reflectance distributions . A useful approximation describing
diffuse reflection is the Lambertian model, with a particularly
simple BRDF, which we denote as $F_L$. The outgoing ray intensity,
$\ell_{\texttt{out}}$, is a function only of the surface orientation relative to the
incoming and outgoing ray directions, the wavelength, a scalar surface
reflectance, and the incoming light power:
$$
\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F_{L} \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}} (\lambda), \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \right) = a \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) \left( \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} \right),
$${#eq-lambert}

discrepancies: A translucent wireframe hemisphere and orange draggable handle are added, but the source shows only stylized outgoing green arrows without a dome guide or handle sphere.
The incoming ℓ_in ray is much shorter and starts from a visible point near the plane, whereas the source ray extends far off the top-left edge with a long yellow-to-red shaft.
The output formula label is placed close to the central vectors and partially crowds the n/q labels; in the source it is large and far to the upper right along the outgoing direction.
The q tangent direction projects downward/foreground in the generated view instead of visually reading as the right/up tangent arrow shown in the source.
The green plane is rendered as a compact diamond-like rectangle rather than the wide shallow parallelogram dominating the source composition.
The sampled outgoing green arrows are more uniform and hemisphere-distributed than the source's stylized translucent lobe arrows clustered around the surface point.
evaluation.notes: The main BRDF geometry and labels are recognizable and the interactions are useful, but added dome/handle elements, altered proportions, and crowded label placement reduce visual fidelity.
action_items: Remove or greatly fade the wireframe hemisphere and draggable handle in the default view to match the original clean schematic.
Lengthen the incoming ray so it enters from far off the upper-left side and make its label larger and higher like the source.
Reposition the formula label far to the upper right and separate it from the n, p, q labels.
Adjust the camera/view and p/q tangent directions so the plane appears as a wide shallow parallelogram and q visually points right/up.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity are strong, but the remaining issues are generator-level visual fidelity problems such as hallucinated guide elements, proportions, label placement, and camera/tangent orientation.
